threads_text: OpenAI released GPT-Rosalind-6, a biology and drug discovery model built on the same weights as GPT-6 Astra, but only approved labs, companies and government partners can use it. OpenAI rates it High for biological risk, so access is the safety feature. Should powerful science AI stay locked behind applications?
caption:
OpenAI released GPT-Rosalind-6 on October 30, a reasoning model for biology and drug discovery.
It runs on the same weights as GPT-6 Astra, but only approved labs, companies and government partners can use it.
On OpenAI's own tests it beat its predecessor by wide margins on drug chemistry and gene tasks.

Should science AI this strong be locked behind an application?

site_article.seo_title: OpenAI GPT-Rosalind-6: biology AI for approved labs only
site_article.seo_description: OpenAI's GPT-Rosalind-6 uses GPT-6 Astra's weights, nearly doubles some biology scores and is open only to vetted organizations.
site_article.answer_summary: GPT-Rosalind-6 is OpenAI's newest model for biology and drug discovery. It is not available in ChatGPT or the general API; only organizations approved through OpenAI's trusted access program can use it.

paragraphs.text: OpenAI released GPT-Rosalind-6 on October 30, 2026, publishing a system card addendum that describes it as a frontier reasoning model for biology, drug discovery and translational medicine. It is the newest model in the GPT-Rosalind line, which OpenAI introduced in April 2026, and it follows GPT-Rosalind-5.5.

According to OpenAI, the model uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra and received no additional training or post-training for this release. The differences are in how it is deployed: who is allowed to use it, and where the line sits between questions it answers and questions it refuses. Its API identifier is gpt-6-rosalind.

OpenAI reported clear gains over GPT-Rosalind-5.5 at the highest reasoning setting it tested. On MedChemBench v7, a set of 99 medicinal chemistry problems, the new model scored 49.6 percent against 28.9 percent. On GeneBench Pro v13, with 129 problems scored on a single attempt, it reached 37.7 percent against 16.7 percent. On LifeSciBench Gold, with 94 problems, it scored 61.3 percent against 44.0 percent.

All of those figures come from OpenAI. Data Studios noted that the problem sets are small and that no independent evaluation had been published at the time of its report, and i-SCOOP likewise said the results had not been reproduced by outside groups.

Under its Preparedness Framework, OpenAI rates GPT-Rosalind-6 High for biological and chemical capability, below the Critical level. The company said none of its four Critical level biological design evaluations met their indicative thresholds. On a biorisk knowledge evaluation the model scored 78.3 percent, slightly below GPT-Rosalind-5.5 at 79.2 percent. The model keeps the Critical cybersecurity rating assessed for GPT-6 Astra, with a more conservative refusal boundary for cyber requests.

OpenAI said the model is meant to answer more legitimate dual-use research questions than its general access models while still refusing requests that would enable severe biological weaponization. The company keeps its biological safety training separate from its classifier training to reduce correlated failures, monitors use, and can restrict or revoke access. It also said biosecurity red teaming carried out on GPT-Rosalind-5.5 was being repeated for the new version.

Access is limited to approved scientists, research institutes, companies and government partners. OpenAI said it reviews each applicant's use case, security controls and governance. Non-government applicants go through business verification and compliance screening, while government applicants use a separate pathway covering biosecurity, biosafety, public health preparedness and biodefense. Data Studios reported that ChatGPT subscribers and general API developers cannot use the model.

Approved enterprise customers must apply least privilege access controls and have qualified people review outputs before those outputs inform experiments, publications or decisions. i-SCOOP reported that no official price for gpt-6-rosalind had been published as of October 31, while earlier Rosalind research models were listed at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens.

The release shows OpenAI treating access itself as a safety tool. Because the weights are identical to GPT-6 Astra, the main thing separating the two products is a vetting process and a different refusal policy. That makes the strength of OpenAI's screening and monitoring as important as the model's test scores, and it leaves the company deciding which organizations get its most capable biology tools.

The next signal to watch is independent evaluation: whether outside labs or approved customers publish results that confirm OpenAI's reported gains on medicinal chemistry and genetics tasks, and whether OpenAI publishes official pricing for the model.
